source.title: Multi-Agent Sampling: Scaling Inference Compute for Data Synthesis with Tree Search-Based Agentic Collaboration
source.authors: Hai Ye; Mingbao Lin; Hwee Tou Ng; Shuicheng Yan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some plotted data are available only as figures without extractable numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling of inference-time compute in a new setting: multi-agent sampling across several language-model tasks, rather than pretraining loss as a function of model parameters, tokens, or training compute.
record.gate_note: The study varies the number of inference-time samples and measures task scores or reward-model scores against inference FLOPs. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, pretraining scaling, or a compute-optimal split between training parameters and tokens.
record.test_reason: The study scales inference-time sampling (number of samples, FLOPs per prompt) across fixed, already-trained models. It mostly compares its TOA orchestration method with other sampling methods. It never varies parameters, training tokens or training compute, and never measures held-out loss. V6 concerns downstream performance as a function of model or pretraining scale, or pretraining loss. Inference-compute scaling of best-of-N reward is a related but different construct. Small (7–9B) and large (70B+) model groups are run on different tasks and are not compared as a size axis. Kaplan is cited as background, and Hoffmann's FLOP-counting method is borrowed only for cost accounting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that multi-agent sampling generally beats single-model sampling as inference compute scales, and that TOA is the most compute-efficient method. TOA reaches 72.2% LC win rate on AlpacaEval and SOTA on WMT, and its synthetic data improves fine-tuning. They report reward hacking under reward-model guidance. They also find that combining four small models on MATH does not beat combining the top two. Their 'scaling laws' refer to inference compute, not pretraining.
record.recipe_differences: Uses inference-time best-of-N sampling across distinct instruction/chat models, with reward-guided tree search and task scores; it does not train language models or measure held-out pretraining loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Reward-model choice affects the apparent scaling outcome: WMT scores improve with compute under KIWI guidance but later decline under KIWI-XXL evaluation. For TOA tree depth, the study reports that greater depth helps with 640 samples, while smaller depth works better with 64 samples (Figure 12).

fits_no_version.finding: For multi-agent best-of-N sampling, reward rises with inference FLOPs. The TOA curve on AlpacaEval is fitted as R = a·log10(C)^2 + b·log10(C) + c with a=-0.0031, b=0.11, c=-0.71. Under an external evaluator, WMT scores rise then fall (reward hacking).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time (test-time) compute scaling: task performance of sampling/search improves smoothly with inference FLOPs, but can saturate or reverse under reward-model hacking.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported results. Several scaling curves are provided as figures without numerical values. AlpacaEval and the WMT test set are randomly down-sampled to 200 prompts/samples for the main plots. The paper itself reports reward hacking: scores under the external KIWI-XXL evaluator decline after initially improving.
record.rows_left_out: Other fixed-sample task scores and fine-tuning results in Tables 1–3 and 6–7 are not separately recorded because they do not show performance as inference compute varies. Additional ablations and plots (Figures 11–14) are not separately cataloged beyond the reported tree-depth sensitivity.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation of pretraining fits.
All: no architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All: no other modality or training regime scaled. Fine-tuning on synthetic data is not scaled.
All: downstream performance is not related to model scale or pretraining loss. Only inference sample count varies.
All: no pretraining exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests with a V6 'supports' label is not justified. 'Scale' in V6 means model or pretraining scale, while this paper varies only inference sample count. All rows are relinked to none and the labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Whether power-law fits from small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation during training.
Effects of depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream task and reward scores against inference-time compute, not performance against parameter scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or training compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices or setup.
